headline: A 550-year-old arch fell into the Pacific
summary: The Hōlei Sea Arch, 90 feet of lava rock at the end of Chain of Craters Road in Volcanoes National Park, has fallen into the Pacific. It was standing on 23 September and gone by 27 September. The park was shut for Tropical Storm Nolo, so nobody saw it go. The park service warned in 2021 that it would crumble one day.

cover_question.q: Why did the arch fall down?

cover_answer: Years of waves and quakes. It went during a storm.
table_question: If a place you love won't last, do you visit more or less?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A huge rock arch in Hawaii, as tall as a nine-floor building, stood over the ocean for 550 years. Last week it fell into the sea. Waves had been nibbling at it for years, the way they flatten a sandcastle. Nobody was near it. The park was shut for a storm, and the lookout had been moved back long ago.
5-7.why: A sandcastle they have watched go. Nothing here to fear.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the sandcastle does the work: waves, a little at a time, then gone. The frightening feature, a giant rock falling, is defused by the shut park and the moved lookout. Expect "could it fall on me?" No. It is already in the sea, and the lookout moved years ago.

8-12.script: The arch was lava rock, 90 feet tall, and the ocean had worked on it for 550 years. Earthquakes in 2018 cracked the cliffs. In 2020 storm waves broke a chunk off the bottom, so the park moved the lookout back. Last weekend, in another storm, it fell. A loose tooth: wiggle, wiggle, gone.
8-12.why: Quakes, waves, storm, gone. A chain they can follow.
8-12.why_long: This age is building chains of cause and effect: quakes in 2018, a chunk lost to waves in 2020, a storm weekend to finish it. The loose tooth is the mechanism: it loosens in steps and goes all at once. Expect "why didn't they fix it?" You cannot prop up a sea cliff. You move the people back. The park did.

13-17.script: In 2021 the park service called the arch "beautiful, but temporary" and said it would fall. It did, 550 years in, during a storm. Does knowing a place is on the clock change whether you go? Second: thousands posted photos of it within a day. Is a photo of something gone worth more, or less?
13-17.why: Temporary, and they said so. What is a visit worth?
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the park called the arch temporary five years before it fell, and thousands still mourned it online. The script hands them both and asks what a visit is worth. Expect "is Hawaii falling into the sea?" Slowly, at the edge, and the park says new arches will form as it goes.

5-7.a: No. The park was closed for a storm, and the path had been moved back years ago. Nobody was near it.

8-12.q: Why did the arch fall down?
8-12.a: Centuries of waves, a 2018 earthquake, then a storm last weekend.
The park says yes. The waves carve new ones as the cliff wears back.

13-17.a: No. A lava cliff against the Pacific. They moved the lookout back in 2020.

13-17.q: Why does anyone care about a rock?
13-17.a: Thousands posted photos within a day. A place you stood is part of your story.
